claim: JC polyomavirus (JCPyV) causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a life-threatening brain disease in immunocompromised patients.
source: JC polyomavirus (JCPyV) causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a life-threatening brain disease in immunocompromised patients.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about JCPyV and PML.

claim: Inherited and acquired T cell deficiencies are associated with PML.
source: Inherited and acquired T cell deficiencies are associated with PML.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about PML risk factors.

claim: The incidence of PML is increasing with the introduction of new immunomodulatory agents, several of which target T cells or B cells.
source: The incidence of PML is increasing with the introduction of new immunomodulatory agents, several of which target T cells or B cells.
evidence: This is a general observation about PML epidemiology in the context of modern immunotherapy.

claim: PML patients often carry mutations in the JCPyV VP1 capsid protein, which confer resistance to neutralizing VP1 antibodies (Ab).
source: PML patients often carry mutations in the JCPyV VP1 capsid protein, which confer resistance to neutralizing VP1 antibodies (Ab).
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript and established knowledge about JCPyV mutations in PML.

claim: Polyomaviruses (PyV) are tightly species-specific.
source: Polyomaviruses (PyV) are tightly species-specific; the absence of tractable animal models has handicapped understanding PyV pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a well-known characteristic of polyomaviruses.

claim: The absence of tractable animal models has handicapped understanding PyV pathogenesis.
source: Polyomaviruses (PyV) are tightly species-specific; the absence of tractable animal models has handicapped understanding PyV pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the species-specificity of polyomaviruses.

claim: T cell deficiency during persistent infection, in the setting of monospecific VP1 Ab, was required for outgrowth of VP1 Ab-escape viral variants in mouse polyomavirus (MuPyV) infection.
source: Using mouse polyomavirus (MuPyV), we found that T cell deficiency during persistent infection, in the setting of monospecific VP1 Ab, was required for outgrowth of VP1 Ab-escape viral variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: CD4 T cells were primarily responsible for limiting polyomavirus infection in the kidney.
source: CD4 T cells were primarily responsible for limiting polyomavirus infection in the kidney, a major reservoir of persistent infection by both JCPyV and MuPyV, and checking emergence of these mutant viruses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing higher kidney virus levels in CD4-depleted mice.

claim: The kidney is a major reservoir of persistent infection by both JCPyV and MuPyV.
source: CD4 T cells were primarily responsible for limiting polyomavirus infection in the kidney, a major reservoir of persistent infection by both JCPyV and MuPyV, and checking emergence of these mutant viruses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about polyomavirus persistence.

claim: T cells provided a second line of defense by controlling the outgrowth of VP1 mutant viruses that evaded Ab neutralization.
source: T cells also provided a second line of defense by controlling the outgrowth of VP1 mutant viruses that evaded Ab neutralization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing viremia in T cell-depleted mice challenged with Ab-escape mutant virus.

claim: A virus with two capsid mutations, one conferring Ab-escape yet impaired infectivity and a second compensatory mutation, yielded a highly neurovirulent variant.
source: A virus with two capsid mutations, one conferring Ab-escape yet impaired infectivity and a second compensatory mutation, yielded a highly neurovirulent variant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on the A2.D295N/Δ297 double mutant virus.

claim: T cell deficiency and evolution of Ab-escape polyomavirus VP1 variants are linked with neuropathogenicity.
source: These findings link T cell deficiency and evolution of Ab-escape polyomavirus VP1 variants with neuropathogenicity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Antibodies (Ab) are critical components of immune defense against viral pathogens and key mediators of immune control during persistent infections.
source: Antibodies (Ab) are critical components of immune defense against viral pathogens and key mediators of immune control during persistent infections.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: Evasion of antibodies, particularly in settings of limited antibody diversity, is a potent selective pressure for viral mutations.
source: Evasion of antibodies, particularly in settings of limited antibody diversity, is a potent selective pressure for viral mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations and general knowledge about viral evolution.

claim: Outgrowth of escape variants is an Achilles' heel for monoclonal antibody (mAb) antiviral intervention.
source: Notably, outgrowth of escape variants is an Achilles' heel for monoclonal antibody (mAb) antiviral intervention (Bar et al., 2016; Caskey et al., 2015; Caskey et al., 2017; Mehandru et al., 2007; Toma et al., 2011; Trkola et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Viral evolution within a host gives rise to variants that become subject to selection for resistance to antiviral antibodies.
source: Viral evolution within a host gives rise to variants that become subject to selection for resistance to antiviral antibodies (Inuzuka et al., 2018; Kinchen et al., 2018; Lynch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Polyomaviruses persist lifelong in their hosts in a 'smoldering' infectious state.
source: For viruses that establish persistent infection, viral variants can accumulate over time and increase the likelihood for emergence of viruses carrying mutations that escape recognition by neutralizing Ab. Polyomaviruses (PyV) persist lifelong in their hosts in a 'smoldering' infectious state, a lifestyle conducive for viral evolution even by a DNA virus that commandeers the high-fidelity host cell DNA polymerase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about polyomavirus biology.

claim: The human BK and JC polyomaviruses have been shown to exist as quasispecies.
source: Indeed, the human BK and JC polyomaviruses have been shown to exist as quasispecies (Luo et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2016; Van Loy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: JCPyV causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a frequently fatal demyelinating brain disease associated with T cell immunosuppression.
source: JCPyV causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a frequently fatal demyelinating brain disease associated with T cell immunosuppression resulting from HIV/AIDS, organ transplant immunosuppressants, and certain chemotherapeutic and immunomodulatory therapies (Cortese et al., 2021; Pavlovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge about PML.

claim: PML is associated with T cell immunosuppression resulting from HIV/AIDS, organ transplant immunosuppressants, and certain chemotherapeutic and immunomodulatory therapies.
source: JCPyV causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a frequently fatal demyelinating brain disease associated with T cell immunosuppression resulting from HIV/AIDS, organ transplant immunosuppressants, and certain chemotherapeutic and immunomodulatory therapies (Cortese et al., 2021; Pavlovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PML is typically identified by MRI following the onset of neurologic symptoms.
source: Typically identified by MRI following the onset of neurologic symptoms, PML is diagnosed at a point when limited treatment options exist and patients suffer permanent CNS damage.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PML diagnosis.

claim: PML is diagnosed at a point when limited treatment options exist and patients suffer permanent CNS damage.
source: Typically identified by MRI following the onset of neurologic symptoms, PML is diagnosed at a point when limited treatment options exist and patients suffer permanent CNS damage.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PML prognosis.

claim: Prolonged immune suppression is a necessary antecedent for PML.
source: Prolonged immune suppression is a necessary antecedent for PML.
evidence: This is supported by clinical observations and citations.

claim: High risk for natalizumab-associated PML involves infusion therapy for >24 months and a history of immunosuppression.
source: For instance, high risk for natalizumab-associated PML involves infusion therapy for >24 months and a history of immunosuppression (Berger and Fox, 2016; Bloomgren et al., 2012; Fox and Rudick, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Iatrogenic T cell and B cell ablation therapies have independently been associated with PML.
source: Iatrogenic T cell and B cell ablation therapies have independently been associated with PML.
evidence: This is supported by clinical observations.

claim: PML is characterized by emergence of mutations in the major capsid protein, VP1, of JCPyV, which are not found in the circulating (i.e., archetype) strains.
source: PML is characterized by emergence of mutations in the major capsid protein, VP1, of JCPyV, which are not found in the circulating (i.e., archetype) strains (Gorelik et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2005b; Zheng et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nonenveloped icosahedral viral capsid is comprised of the VP1 protein assembled into 72 pentamers.
source: The nonenveloped icosahedral viral capsid is comprised of the VP1 protein assembled into 72 pentamers.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about polyomavirus capsids.

claim: VP1 mediates attachment to cellular receptors via its four solvent-exposed loops.
source: VP1 mediates attachment to cellular receptors via its four solvent-exposed loops; these loops are also the dominant targets of the host's neutralizing Ab response (Buch et al., 2015; Lindner et al., 2019; Neu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The four solvent-exposed loops of VP1 are the dominant targets of the host's neutralizing Ab response.
source: VP1 mediates attachment to cellular receptors via its four solvent-exposed loops; these loops are also the dominant targets of the host's neutralizing Ab response (Buch et al., 2015; Lindner et al., 2019; Neu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations are situated in the solvent-exposed loops of VP1.
source: JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations, which are situated in these loops, mediate resistance to neutralizing antibodies, but also alter receptor binding and viral tropism (Geoghegan et al., 2017; Gorelik et al., 2011; Jelcic et al., 2015; Lauver et al., 2020; Maginnis et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations mediate resistance to neutralizing antibodies.
source: JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations, which are situated in these loops, mediate resistance to neutralizing antibodies, but also alter receptor binding and viral tropism (Geoghegan et al., 2017; Gorelik et al., 2011; Jelcic et al., 2015; Lauver et al., 2020; Maginnis et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations alter receptor binding and viral tropism.
source: JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations, which are situated in these loops, mediate resistance to neutralizing antibodies, but also alter receptor binding and viral tropism (Geoghegan et al., 2017; Gorelik et al., 2011; Jelcic et al., 2015; Lauver et al., 2020; Maginnis et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sera from PML patients fail to neutralize particular JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations, despite these individuals having high antibody titers against WT JCPyV.
source: Sera from PML patients, as well as some healthy individuals, fail to neutralize particular JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations, despite these individuals having high antibody titers against WT JCPyV (Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sera from some healthy individuals fail to neutralize particular JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations, despite these individuals having high antibody titers against WT JCPyV.
source: Sera from PML patients, as well as some healthy individuals, fail to neutralize particular JCPyV-PML VP1 mutations, despite these individuals having high antibody titers against WT JCPyV (Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MuPyV shares several features with JCPyV, including asymptomatic disease in immunocompetent hosts, the kidney as a dominant reservoir of virus persistence, and control by virus-specific T cells.
source: MuPyV shares several features with JCPyV, including asymptomatic disease in immunocompetent hosts, the kidney as a dominant reservoir of virus persistence, and control by virus-specific T cells.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The attachment receptor for JCPyV is the oligosaccharide lactoseries tetrasaccharide c.
source: Although both viruses bind to cell surface sialylated glycan receptors, the attachment receptor for JCPyV is the oligosaccharide lactoseries tetrasaccharide c, whereas MuPyV binds the gangliosides GD1a and GT1b (Buch et al., 2015; Neu et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MuPyV binds the gangliosides GD1a and GT1b.
source: Although both viruses bind to cell surface sialylated glycan receptors, the attachment receptor for JCPyV is the oligosaccharide lactoseries tetrasaccharide c, whereas MuPyV binds the gangliosides GD1a and GT1b (Buch et al., 2015; Neu et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A neutralizing mAb against MuPyV VP1 was previously identified.
source: We previously identified a neutralizing mAb against MuPyV VP1 (Swimm et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The epitope for the VP1 mAb is the dominant target of the endogenous VP1 Ab response in mice.
source: The epitope for this mAb is the dominant target of the endogenous VP1 Ab response in mice.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work.

claim: The VP1 mAb failed to recognize several VP1 mutations introduced into WT MuPyV that mapped to mutations seen in JCPyV isolates from PML patients.
source: Importantly, this mAb failed to recognize several VP1 mutations introduced into WT MuPyV that mapped to mutations seen in JCPyV isolates from PML patients (Lauver et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: μMT mice infected subcutaneously via the hind footpad developed high-titer chronic viremia.
source: μMT mice infected subcutaneously (s.c.) via the hind footpad developed high-titer chronic viremia, which was efficiently controlled by injection of VP1 mAb starting at 4 days post-infection (dpi) and continuing weekly thereafter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: High-titer chronic viremia in μMT mice was efficiently controlled by injection of VP1 mAb starting at 4 days post-infection (dpi) and continuing weekly thereafter.
source: μMT mice infected subcutaneously (s.c.) via the hind footpad developed high-titer chronic viremia, which was efficiently controlled by injection of VP1 mAb starting at 4 days post-infection (dpi) and continuing weekly thereafter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: At 20 dpi, sera of VP1 mAb-treated μMT mice displayed similar neutralizing titers as B6 mice against WT MuPyV.
source: At 20 days post-infection (dpi), sera of VP1 mAb-treated μMT mice displayed similar neutralizing titers as B6 mice against WT MuPyV, but an inability to neutralize a published VP1 mutant virus with a deletion of aspartic acid at position 295, A2.Δ295.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: At 20 dpi, sera of VP1 mAb-treated μMT mice showed an inability to neutralize A2.Δ295.
source: At 20 days post-infection (dpi), sera of VP1 mAb-treated μMT mice displayed similar neutralizing titers as B6 mice against WT MuPyV, but an inability to neutralize a published VP1 mutant virus with a deletion of aspartic acid at position 295, A2.Δ295.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: A2.Δ295 was previously isolated following passage of WT virus in the presence of the VP1 mAb and identified as being resistant to neutralization.
source: A virus carrying this mutation was previously isolated following passage of WT virus in the presence of the VP1 mAb and identified as being resistant to neutralization (Lauver et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: At 30 dpi, no significant differences were observed in the numbers of kidney infiltrating T cells in WT and VP1-mAb-treated μMT mice.
source: At 30 dpi, no significant differences were observed in the numbers of kidney infiltrating T cells in WT and VP1-mAb-treated μMT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Ten days after starting T cell depletion, CD4 and CD8 T cells were absent from the blood of depleted mice.
source: Ten days after starting T cell depletion, CD4 and CD8 T cells were absent from the blood of depleted mice and virus levels were significantly elevated in the kidney, the dominant site of MuPyV persistent infection, (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ten days after starting T cell depletion, virus levels were significantly elevated in the kidney.
source: Ten days after starting T cell depletion, CD4 and CD8 T cells were absent from the blood of depleted mice and virus levels were significantly elevated in the kidney, the dominant site of MuPyV persistent infection, (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In mice receiving CD4 or CD8β T-cell-depleting antibodies individually, kidney virus levels were increased in CD4, but not CD8β, T-cell-depleted mice.
source: In mice receiving CD4 or CD8β T-cell-depleting antibodies individually, kidney virus levels were increased in CD4, but not CD8β, T-cell-depleted mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In dual CD4 and CD8 T-cell-depleted mice, anti-VP1 immunofluorescence staining was localized to disrupted tubules expressing Tamm-Horsfall protein (THP).
source: In dual CD4 and CD8 T-cell-depleted mice, anti-VP1 immunofluorescence staining was localized to disrupted tubules expressing Tamm-Horsfall protein (THP), identifying the distal convoluted tubules as a major site of MuPyV replication in the kidney (Tokonami et al., 2018; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and a citation.

claim: The distal convoluted tubules are a major site of MuPyV replication in the kidney.
source: In dual CD4 and CD8 T-cell-depleted mice, anti-VP1 immunofluorescence staining was localized to disrupted tubules expressing Tamm-Horsfall protein (THP), identifying the distal convoluted tubules as a major site of MuPyV replication in the kidney (Tokonami et al., 2018; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of VP1 staining to THP+ tubules and supported by a citation.

claim: Viremia became detectable in CD4 and CD8β T-cell-depleted mice as early as 40 days after dual CD4 and CD8 T cell depletion.
source: Viremia became detectable in CD4 and CD8β T-cell-depleted mice as early as 40 days after dual CD4 and CD8 T cell depletion, with all mice developing viremia by approximately 100 days post depletion.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All CD4 and CD8β T-cell-depleted mice developed viremia by approximately 100 days post depletion.
source: Viremia became detectable in CD4 and CD8β T-cell-depleted mice as early as 40 days after dual CD4 and CD8 T cell depletion, with all mice developing viremia by approximately 100 days post depletion.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CD4 T cell loss alone led to viremia in all mice by 120 days post depletion.
source: CD4 T cell loss alone also led to viremia in all mice by 120 days post depletion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fewer than half of persistently infected mice given control IgG or CD8β T-cell-depleting antibody became viremic.
source: In contrast, fewer than half of persistently infected mice given control IgG or CD8β T-cell-depleting antibody became viremic; in IgG-treated mice the development of viremia was delayed and peaked at approximately 100-fold lower levels than the T cell-depleted mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In IgG-treated mice the development of viremia was delayed and peaked at approximately 100-fold lower levels than the T cell-depleted mice.
source: In contrast, fewer than half of persistently infected mice given control IgG or CD8β T-cell-depleting antibody became viremic; in IgG-treated mice the development of viremia was delayed and peaked at approximately 100-fold lower levels than the T cell-depleted mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mice receiving combined CD4 and CD8 T cell depletion or CD4 T cell depletion alone showed high systemic viral infection in the kidney, spleen, and brain.
source: Mice receiving combined CD4 and CD8 T cell depletion or CD4 T cell depletion alone showed high systemic viral infection in the kidney, spleen, and brain (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: Sequencing plaque-purified virus from the blood of each viremic mouse revealed mutations in VP1, with typically only one VP1 variant found in individual mice.
source: Sequencing plaque-purified virus from the blood of each viremic mouse revealed mutations in VP1, with typically only one VP1 variant found in individual mice (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: A PML patient typically harbors a single VP1 mutant JCPyV in their CSF, brain, and blood.
source: This finding mirrors evidence that a PML patient typically harbors a single VP1 mutant JCPyV in their CSF, brain, and blood (Gorelik et al., 2011; Reid et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Δ295 was the most frequently detected mutation in viremic mice.
source: Several of these non-synonymous single nucleotide substitutions and codon deletions were previously isolated from serially passaged MuPyV refractory to VP1 mAb-mediated neutralization, including Δ295, the most frequently detected mutation, as well as V296F, previously identified as the MuPyV equivalent of the common JCPyV PML mutation S268F (Lauver et al., 2020; Sunyaev et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: V296F was previously identified as the MuPyV equivalent of the common JCPyV PML mutation S268F.
source: Several of these non-synonymous single nucleotide substitutions and codon deletions were previously isolated from serially passaged MuPyV refractory to VP1 mAb-mediated neutralization, including Δ295, the most frequently detected mutation, as well as V296F, previously identified as the MuPyV equivalent of the common JCPyV PML mutation S268F (Lauver et al., 2020; Sunyaev et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Each of the VP1 mutant viruses contained a mutation in the HI loop, where the heavy chain of the VP1 mAb contacts multiple residues.
source: Each of the VP1 mutant viruses contained a mutation in the HI loop, where the heavy chain of the VP1 mAb contacts multiple residues (Figure 3A; Lauver et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A and a citation.

claim: VP1 mutations introduced into WT MuPyV using site-directed mutagenesis blocked neutralization by the VP1 mAb.
source: To exclude possible effects of other mutations in the viral genome, we introduced several of these single and dual VP1 mutations into WT MuPyV using site-directed mutagenesis. We found that these mutations blocked neutralization by the VP1 mAb (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The VP1 mutations had varying effects on the efficiency of viral infection in the kidney and spleen.
source: Despite the shared resistance to neutralization, the mutations had varying effects on the efficiency of viral infection in the kidney and spleen (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C–D.

claim: Escape from neutralizing antibody, not shifts in tissue tropism, was the selective pressure behind the emergence of VP1 mutations in vivo.
source: These data indicate that escape from neutralizing antibody, not shifts in tissue tropism, was the selective pressure behind the emergence of VP1 mutations in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that all mutations conferred antibody resistance despite varying effects on tropism.

claim: Mice receiving CD4 and CD8β T-cell-depleting antibodies developed viremia with progressively increasing infectious virus titers over time after challenge with A2.Δ295.
source: Mice receiving CD4 and CD8β T-cell-depleting antibodies developed viremia with progressively increasing infectious virus titers over time; in contrast, no viremia was detected in the control IgG-treated mice (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No viremia was detected in control IgG-treated mice after challenge with A2.Δ295.
source: Mice receiving CD4 and CD8β T-cell-depleting antibodies developed viremia with progressively increasing infectious virus titers over time; in contrast, no viremia was detected in the control IgG-treated mice (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: T-cell-depleted mice challenged with A2.Δ295 had 100–1000-fold higher virus levels in the kidney, spleen, and brain than the IgG-treated mice.
source: Moreover, the T-cell-depleted mice had 100–1000-fold higher virus levels in the kidney, spleen, and brain than the IgG-treated mice (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: T cells act to prevent viremia by MuPyV variants that escape neutralizing antibody.
source: These results provide clear evidence that T cells act to prevent viremia by MuPyV variants that escape neutralizing antibody.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing no viremia in IgG-treated mice but viremia in T cell-depleted mice after challenge with Ab-escape mutant.

claim: A2.D295N remained sensitive to neutralization by VP1 mAb.
source: Neutralization assays with VP1 mAb showed that A2.D295N remained sensitive, but A2.Δ297 was fully resistant, to neutralization (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A2.Δ297 was fully resistant to neutralization by VP1 mAb.
source: Neutralization assays with VP1 mAb showed that A2.D295N remained sensitive, but A2.Δ297 was fully resistant, to neutralization (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A2.D295N was readily bound by the VP1 mAb.
source: Similar to parental A2, A2.D295N was readily bound by the VP1 mAb; in contrast, the mAb did not bind A2.Δ297 or A2.D295N/Δ297 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The VP1 mAb did not bind A2.Δ297 or A2.D295N/Δ297.
source: Similar to parental A2, A2.D295N was readily bound by the VP1 mAb; in contrast, the mAb did not bind A2.Δ297 or A2.D295N/Δ297 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A2.D295N showed a similar avidity profile to parental A2 with the VP1 mAb.
source: A2.D295N also showed a similar avidity profile to parental A2 with the VP1 mAb (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: D295N did not affect neutralization.
source: Taken together, these data show that D295N did not affect neutralization, suggesting that this mutation did not contribute to antibody escape.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the neutralization and binding data.

claim: A2.Δ297 failed to form plaques.
source: In support, we found that A2.Δ297 failed to form plaques, indicating a defect in spread (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A2.D295N formed plaques comparably to WT virus.
source: In contrast, A2.D295N formed plaques comparably to WT virus and A2.D295N/Δ297 produced significantly smaller sized plaques.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A2.D295N/Δ297 produced significantly smaller sized plaques than WT virus.
source: In contrast, A2.D295N formed plaques comparably to WT virus and A2.D295N/Δ297 produced significantly smaller sized plaques.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reduced plaque size by MuPyV has been associated with increased affinity for binding host cell receptors.
source: Reduced plaque size by MuPyV has been associated with increased affinity for binding host cell receptors (Bauer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A2.D295N showed decreased virion production.
source: By titering infectious virus output during one round of replication by plaque assay, we observed decreased virion production by A2.D295N but significantly increased replication by A2.D295N/Δ297 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A2.D295N/Δ297 showed significantly increased replication compared to WT.
source: By titering infectious virus output during one round of replication by plaque assay, we observed decreased virion production by A2.D295N but significantly increased replication by A2.D295N/Δ297 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A2.D295N/Δ297 showed enhanced infection compared to A2.
source: Matching virus titers by DNA genome equivalents (g.e.), we found enhanced infection by A2.D295N/Δ297, whereas A2.Δ297 had similar infectivity to A2 and A2.D295N had reduced infectivity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A2.Δ297 had similar infectivity to A2.
source: Matching virus titers by DNA genome equivalents (g.e.), we found enhanced infection by A2.D295N/Δ297, whereas A2.Δ297 had similar infectivity to A2 and A2.D295N had reduced infectivity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A2.D295N had reduced infectivity compared to A2.
source: Matching virus titers by DNA genome equivalents (g.e.), we found enhanced infection by A2.D295N/Δ297, whereas A2.Δ297 had similar infectivity to A2 and A2.D295N had reduced infectivity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A2.Δ297 and A2.D295N both showed a significant reduction in spread compared to A2.
source: Using a low multiplicity of infection (MOI) infection to track viral spread, we found that A2.Δ297 and A2.D295N both showed a significant reduction in spread compared to A2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cells transfected with equal amounts of viral DNA showed similar levels of virus output at 72 hr by A2.D295N and A2.Δ297.
source: This reduction in spread was not due to reduced virus production; cells transfected with equal amounts of viral DNA showed similar levels of virus output at 72 hr by A2.D295N and A2.Δ297, but significantly more virus by A2.D295N/Δ297 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells transfected with equal amounts of viral DNA showed significantly more virus output at 72 hr by A2.D295N/Δ297 compared to A2.D295N and A2.Δ297.
source: This reduction in spread was not due to reduced virus production; cells transfected with equal amounts of viral DNA showed similar levels of virus output at 72 hr by A2.D295N and A2.Δ297, but significantly more virus by A2.D295N/Δ297 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Δ297 mutation impaired viral spread and prevented plaque formation.
source: These data indicate the Δ297 mutation impaired viral spread and prevented plaque formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the plaque assay and spread data.

claim: The D295N mutation impaired both virus infection and spread but remained able to form plaques over the course of the 6-day plaque assay.
source: In contrast, the D295N mutation impaired both virus infection and spread but remained able to form plaques over the course of the 6-day plaque assay.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the plaque assay, infectivity, and spread data.

claim: In combination, the D295N and Δ297 mutations showed a restoration and even enhancement of infectivity and spread.
source: In combination, however, these mutations showed a restoration and even enhancement of infectivity and spread.
evidence: This is supported by the data on the double mutant virus.

claim: Parental A2 and A2.D295N/Δ297 showed preferential hemagglutination (HA) activity at acidic pH.
source: Parental A2 and A2.D295N/Δ297 showed preferential hemagglutination (HA) activity at acidic pH (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A2.D295N and A2.Δ297 exhibited poor HA activity.
source: A2.D295N and A2.Δ297 exhibited poor HA activity, with A2.Δ297 showing no HA activity across the pH spectrum.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A2.Δ297 showed no HA activity across the pH spectrum.
source: A2.D295N and A2.Δ297 exhibited poor HA activity, with A2.Δ297 showing no HA activity across the pH spectrum.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Binding by A2, A2.Δ297, and A2.D295N/Δ297 was dependent on sialylated host cell receptors.
source: Binding by A2, A2.Δ297, and A2.D295N/Δ297 was dependent on sialylated host cell receptors, but binding by A2.D295N was refractory to neuraminidase treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Binding by A2.D295N was refractory to neuraminidase treatment.
source: Binding by A2, A2.Δ297, and A2.D295N/Δ297 was dependent on sialylated host cell receptors, but binding by A2.D295N was refractory to neuraminidase treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Neuraminidase pretreatment caused a significant reduction in LT mRNA levels and T ag+ cells for all viruses, indicating that infection by all viruses relied predominantly on a sialic-acid-dependent pathway.
source: Despite these differences in binding, neuraminidase pretreatment caused a significant reduction 24 hpi in LT mRNA levels with low MOI infection and T ag+ cells with high MOI infection, indicating that infection by all viruses relied predominantly on a sialic-acid-dependent pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: The D295N mutation mediated binding to a non-sialylated, non-productive receptor.
source: The dependence on sialic acid for infection, but not for binding, by A2.D295N indicates that by itself the D295N mutation mediated binding to a non-sialylated, non-productive receptor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the neuraminidase treatment data.

claim: The A2.Δ297 single mutant showed a drastic sensitivity to neuraminidase pretreatment, with 10,000-fold reduction in mRNA production.
source: In contrast, the A2.Δ297 single mutant showed a drastic sensitivity to neuraminidase pretreatment, with 10,000-fold reduction in mRNA production, consistent with poor receptor binding and the lack of HA activity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Parental A2 bound to the lumen of the distal convoluted tubules (DCT).
source: Parental A2 bound to the lumen of the distal convoluted tubules (DCT) and binding was abrogated by neuraminidase pretreatment (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A2 binding to the DCT was abrogated by neuraminidase pretreatment.
source: Parental A2 bound to the lumen of the distal convoluted tubules (DCT) and binding was abrogated by neuraminidase pretreatment (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A2.D295N/Δ297 showed specific, neuraminidase-sensitive binding to the DCT.
source: Similar to A2, the A2.D295N/Δ297 showed specific, neuraminidase-sensitive binding to the DCT.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A2.Δ297 showed no detectable binding in the kidney.
source: A2.Δ297, however, showed no detectable binding in the kidney, whereas A2.D295N showed substantial binding to the abluminal side of the tubules but little-to no-binding to the luminal side.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A2.D295N showed substantial binding to the abluminal side of the tubules but little-to no-binding to the luminal side.
source: A2.Δ297, however, showed no detectable binding in the kidney, whereas A2.D295N showed substantial binding to the abluminal side of the tubules but little-to no-binding to the luminal side.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A2.D295N binding in the kidney was insensitive to neuraminidase treatment.
source: A2.D295N binding in the kidney was insensitive to neuraminidase treatment.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Both A2.Δ297 and A2.D295N single mutant viruses were attenuated in the kidney compared to A2 at 4 dpi.
source: We then assessed virus levels in the kidneys of mice infected i.v. with the mutant viruses. Based on LT mRNA levels in the kidney at 4 dpi, both single mutant viruses were attenuated compared to A2, whereas A2.D295N/Δ297 showed similar levels of infection to A2 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: A2.D295N/Δ297 showed similar levels of infection to A2 in the kidney at 4 dpi.
source: We then assessed virus levels in the kidneys of mice infected i.v. with the mutant viruses. Based on LT mRNA levels in the kidney at 4 dpi, both single mutant viruses were attenuated compared to A2, whereas A2.D295N/Δ297 showed similar levels of infection to A2 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The Δ297 mutation conferred resistance to VP1 mAb neutralization, but impaired viral spread and infection within the kidney.
source: Together, these findings indicate that the Δ297 mutation conferred resistance to VP1 mAb neutralization, but impaired viral spread and infection within the kidney.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: The D295N mutation alone caused aberrant receptor binding and impaired infection in vivo.
source: The D295N mutation alone caused aberrant receptor binding and impaired infection in vivo, but when combined with Δ297 restored proper receptor binding in the kidney during early infection.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: When combined with Δ297, the D295N mutation restored proper receptor binding in the kidney during early infection.
source: The D295N mutation alone caused aberrant receptor binding and impaired infection in vivo, but when combined with Δ297 restored proper receptor binding in the kidney during early infection.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: Ab escape by the Δ297 mutation was the initial driver of mutant virus emergence in vivo, with the emergence of the mutation at D295 occurring secondary to compensate for the defect in virulence.
source: Based on the effects of the D295N and Δ297 mutations, we hypothesized that Ab escape by the Δ297 mutation was the initial driver of mutant virus emergence in vivo, with the emergence of the mutation at D295 occurring secondary to compensate for the defect in virulence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the functional characterization of the mutations.

claim: In 50 clones sequenced from the kidneys of each of three mice that developed double mutant viruses, sequences containing WT VP1, Δ297, and D295N/Δ297 or D295A/Δ297 were identified, but not sequences containing the D295N/A mutations alone.
source: In 50 clones sequenced from the kidneys of each of the three mice, we identified sequences containing WT VP1, Δ297, and D295N/Δ297 or D295A/Δ297, but not sequences containing the D295N/A mutations alone (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The presence of the individual Δ297 mutation and absence of single D295 mutations suggests that the initial mutation was Δ297 followed by D295N/A.
source: The presence of the individual Δ297 mutation and absence of single D295 mutations suggests that the initial mutation was Δ297 followed by D295N/A.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sequencing data.

claim: Infection of μMT mice i.v. with A2 or A2.D295N/Δ297 resulted in chronic viremia 30 dpi by each virus.
source: We infected μMT mice i.v. with A2 or A2.D295N/Δ297, which resulted in chronic viremia 30 dpi by each virus (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Kidneys from A2-infected μMT mice had foci of lymphocytic inflammation within the cortical interstitium that extended into the tubular epithelium.
source: Kidneys from A2-infected mice had foci of lymphocytic inflammation within the cortical interstitium that extended into the tubular epithelium (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Kidneys from A2.D295N/Δ297-infected μMT mice had only small, scattered collections of mononuclear cells.
source: In marked contrast, kidneys A2.D295N/Δ297-infected mice had only small, scattered collections of mononuclear cells.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A2-infected kidneys exhibited numerous, large VP1+ foci.
source: Consistent with these histopathologic differences, A2-infected kidneys also exhibited numerous, large VP1+ foci, but those in A2.D295N/Δ297-infected kidneys were far fewer and smaller (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C–D.

claim: VP1+ foci in A2.D295N/Δ297-infected kidneys were far fewer and smaller than in A2-infected kidneys.
source: Consistent with these histopathologic differences, A2-infected kidneys also exhibited numerous, large VP1+ foci, but those in A2.D295N/Δ297-infected kidneys were far fewer and smaller (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C–D.

claim: Four dpi after i.c. infection, A2-infected brains showed only sparse VP1+ ependymal cells lining the ventricles.
source: Four dpi, A2-infected brains showed only sparse VP1+ ependymal cells lining the ventricles. In contrast, brains of A2.D295N/Δ297-infected mice had extensive VP1+ ependymal cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Four dpi after i.c. infection, brains of A2.D295N/Δ297-infected mice had extensive VP1+ ependymal cells.
source: Four dpi, A2-infected brains showed only sparse VP1+ ependymal cells lining the ventricles. In contrast, brains of A2.D295N/Δ297-infected mice had extensive VP1+ ependymal cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A2-infected brains at 30 dpi had only small ependymal lymphocytic aggregates.
source: Consistent with this dramatic difference in extent of ependymal infection, A2-infected brains at 30 dpi had only small ependymal lymphocytic aggregates, whereas A2.D295N/Δ297-infected brains contained more extensive ependymitis as well as periventricular edema (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A2.D295N/Δ297-infected brains at 30 dpi contained more extensive ependymitis as well as periventricular edema.
source: Consistent with this dramatic difference in extent of ependymal infection, A2-infected brains at 30 dpi had only small ependymal lymphocytic aggregates, whereas A2.D295N/Δ297-infected brains contained more extensive ependymitis as well as periventricular edema (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Only brains from mice persistently infected with A2.D295N/Δ297 had VP1+ cells in the periventricular region.
source: Additionally, of the sections examined only brains from mice persistently infected with A2.D295N/Δ297 had VP1+ cells in the periventricular region (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Hydrocephalus is consistently seen in mice i.c. inoculated with A2 MuPyV.
source: Hydrocephalus is consistently seen in mice i.c. inoculated with A2 MuPyV (Lauver et al., 2020; Mockus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A2.D295N/Δ297-infected mice developed hydrocephalus to a significantly higher degree than A2-infected mice.
source: A2.D295N/Δ297-infected mice developed hydrocephalus to a significantly higher degree than A2-infected mice (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The endogenously derived A2.D295N/Δ297 VP1 mutant virus had lower tropism for the kidney than the parental A2 virus.
source: These data show that the endogenously derived A2.D295N/Δ297 VP1 mutant virus had lower tropism for the kidney, but dramatically higher capacity to infect the cerebral ventricular system than the parental A2 virus.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings on kidney and brain infection.

claim: The endogenously derived A2.D295N/Δ297 VP1 mutant virus had dramatically higher capacity to infect the cerebral ventricular system than the parental A2 virus.
source: These data show that the endogenously derived A2.D295N/Δ297 VP1 mutant virus had lower tropism for the kidney, but dramatically higher capacity to infect the cerebral ventricular system than the parental A2 virus.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings on kidney and brain infection.

claim: Impaired kidney pathogenesis but retained neurovirulence is a hallmark feature of A2 virus carrying the VP1 V296F mutation.
source: Similarly, impaired kidney pathogenesis but retained neurovirulence is a hallmark feature of A2 virus carrying the VP1 V296F mutation, sequence-equivalent to the frequent S268F VP1 mutation in JCPyV-PML (Lauver et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: VP1 neutralizing Ab in T-cell-deficient hosts can select rare Ab-escape virus variants possessing high neuropathogenicity.
source: Thus, VP1 neutralizing Ab in T-cell-deficient hosts can select rare Ab-escape virus variants possessing high neuropathogenicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Impaired T cell control results in increased PyV replication in the kidney.
source: First, impaired T cell control results in increase PyV replication in the kidney, the central reservoir for persistent PyV infection.
evidence: This is part of the model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Elevated viral replication is accompanied by low-level, stochastic mutagenesis of the viral genome.
source: Elevated viral replication is accompanied by low-level, stochastic mutagenesis of the viral genome, where particular mutations in VP1 abrogate binding by VP1-specific Ab.
evidence: This is part of the model proposed based on the experimental findings and general knowledge of viral evolution.

claim: A subset of viruses carrying Ab-escape VP1 mutations acquire the capacity to replicate in the CNS.
source: A subset of viruses carrying Ab-escape VP1 mutations acquire the capacity to replicate in the CNS.
evidence: This is part of the model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: T cell deficiency handicaps a second line of defense by antiviral T cells to control Ab-escape VP1 variant viruses.
source: T cell deficiency further handicaps a second line of defense by antiviral T cells to control Ab-escape VP1 variant viruses.
evidence: This is part of the model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: T cell deficiency acts at two levels to set the stage for emergence of antibody-escape VP1 mutations endowed with neurotropic potential.
source: In summary, T cell deficiency acts at two levels to set the stage for emergence of antibody-escape VP1 mutations endowed with neurotropic potential.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The kidney is the major site of JCPyV persistence.
source: The kidney is the major site of JCPyV persistence (Berger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MuPyV preferentially binds to the DCT, mirroring what has been reported for JCPyV.
source: We observed preferential binding of MuPyV to the DCT, mirroring what has been reported for JCPyV, and virus replication in the DCT following T cell loss (Figures 1D and 5G; Haley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1D and 5G and a citation.

claim: Virus replication occurs in the DCT following T cell loss.
source: We observed preferential binding of MuPyV to the DCT, mirroring what has been reported for JCPyV, and virus replication in the DCT following T cell loss (Figures 1D and 5G; Haley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Depressed JCPyV-specific T cell responses are seen in individuals treated with natalizumab.
source: Consistent with this are reports of depressed JCPyV-specific T cell responses in individuals treated with natalizumab and increased JCPyV shedding in the urine of immunosuppressed individuals (Behzad-Behbahani et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2009; Delbue et al., 2015; Perkins et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Increased JCPyV shedding in the urine is seen in immunosuppressed individuals.
source: Consistent with this are reports of depressed JCPyV-specific T cell responses in individuals treated with natalizumab and increased JCPyV shedding in the urine of immunosuppressed individuals (Behzad-Behbahani et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2009; Delbue et al., 2015; Perkins et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T cells are the predominant cell type responsible for the production of interferon gamma (IFN-γ).
source: T cells are the predominant cell type responsible for the production of interferon gamma (IFN-γ), which limits BKPyV replication in kidney cells and is necessary for effective control of MuPyV kidney infection (Abend et al., 2007; Byers et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IFN-γ limits BKPyV replication in kidney cells.
source: T cells are the predominant cell type responsible for the production of interferon gamma (IFN-γ), which limits BKPyV replication in kidney cells and is necessary for effective control of MuPyV kidney infection (Abend et al., 2007; Byers et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IFN-γ is necessary for effective control of MuPyV kidney infection.
source: T cells are the predominant cell type responsible for the production of interferon gamma (IFN-γ), which limits BKPyV replication in kidney cells and is necessary for effective control of MuPyV kidney infection (Abend et al., 2007; Byers et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T cell loss during PyV infection eliminates the major source of IFN-γ and virus control.
source: T cell loss during PyV infection thus eliminates the major source of IFN-γ and virus control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of T cells in IFN-γ production.

claim: PML is associated with conditions of CD4 T cell impairment, including HIV/AIDS and idiopathic CD4 T cell lymphopenia.
source: PML is associated with conditions of CD4 T cell impairment, including HIV/AIDS and idiopathic CD4 T cell lymphopenia (Berger et al., 1987; Berger et al., 1998; Pavlovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Decreases in CD4, but not CD8, T cells are seen in the CSF of natalizumab-treated MS patients.
source: Decreases in CD4, but not CD8, T cells are seen in the CSF of natalizumab-treated MS patients and CD4 T cell epitope-escape JCPyVs have been found in PML patients (Jelcic et al., 2016; Schneider-Hohendorf et al., 2014; Stüve et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD4 T cell epitope-escape JCPyVs have been found in PML patients.
source: Decreases in CD4, but not CD8, T cells are seen in the CSF of natalizumab-treated MS patients and CD4 T cell epitope-escape JCPyVs have been found in PML patients (Jelcic et al., 2016; Schneider-Hohendorf et al., 2014; Stüve et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD4 T cells can exert direct antiviral effector activities.
source: CD4 T cells can exert direct antiviral effector activities as well as provide help to maintain optimal virus-specific CD8 T cell responses in nonlymphoid organs, including the brain and lung (Ren et al., 2020; Son et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD4 T cells provide help to maintain optimal virus-specific CD8 T cell responses in nonlymphoid organs, including the brain and lung.
source: CD4 T cells can exert direct antiviral effector activities as well as provide help to maintain optimal virus-specific CD8 T cell responses in nonlymphoid organs, including the brain and lung (Ren et al., 2020; Son et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tissue-resident CD4 T cells promote development of protective B cell responses in the lungs of influenza virus-infected mice.
source: Tissue-resident CD4 T cells have also been shown to promote development of protective B cell responses in the lungs of influenza virus-infected mice (Son et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PyVs are regarded as having highly stable genomes with a low incidence of mutations.
source: Utilizing the host DNA replication machinery, PyVs are regarded as having highly stable genomes with a low incidence of mutations (Sanjuán and Domingo-Calap, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: JCPyV and BKPyV isolates from PML and polyomavirus-associated nephropathy patients are characterized by mutations in both the VP1 capsid protein and the non-coding control region (NCCR).
source: JCPyV and BKPyV isolates from PML and polyomavirus-associated nephropathy patients, respectively, are characterized by mutations in both the VP1 capsid protein and the non-coding control region (NCCR) (Boldorini et al., 2009; Gorelik et al., 2011; Krautkrämer et al., 2009; Peretti et al., 2018; Reid et al., 2011; Tremolada et al., 2010; Vaz et al., 2000; Zheng et al., 2005b; Zheng et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rearrangements in the NCCR of BKPyV emerge after extended passage in vitro.
source: Likewise, rearrangements in the NCCR of BKPyV emerge after extended passage in vitro, and VP1 mutations arise in BKPyV and MuPyV after serial passage in the presence of neutralizing mAb (Lauver et al., 2020; Lindner et al., 2019; Zhao and Imperiale, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VP1 mutations arise in BKPyV and MuPyV after serial passage in the presence of neutralizing mAb.
source: Likewise, rearrangements in the NCCR of BKPyV emerge after extended passage in vitro, and VP1 mutations arise in BKPyV and MuPyV after serial passage in the presence of neutralizing mAb (Lauver et al., 2020; Lindner et al., 2019; Zhao and Imperiale, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The APOBEC3 family of proteins are cytosine deaminases that induce mutagenic damage in the genomes of DNA viruses as a mechanism of antiviral defense.
source: The APOBEC3 family of proteins are cytosine deaminases that induce mutagenic damage in the genomes of DNA viruses as a mechanism of antiviral defense.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APOBEC3 proteins.

claim: APOBEC3B is upregulated during BKPyV nephritis.
source: APOBEC3B is upregulated during BKPyV nephritis and has been implicated in the emergence of BKPyV VP1 mutations in kidney transplant recipients and mutations in the Merkel cell PyV genome (Peretti et al., 2018; Que et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: APOBEC3B has been implicated in the emergence of BKPyV VP1 mutations in kidney transplant recipients.
source: APOBEC3B is upregulated during BKPyV nephritis and has been implicated in the emergence of BKPyV VP1 mutations in kidney transplant recipients and mutations in the Merkel cell PyV genome (Peretti et al., 2018; Que et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA double strand breaks occur during PyV infection.
source: DNA double strand breaks occur during PyV infection, and aspects of the DNA damage response pathway are required for efficient PyV replication (Erickson and Garcea, 2019; Heiser et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2012; Justice et al., 2019; Sowd et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Aspects of the DNA damage response pathway are required for efficient PyV replication.
source: DNA double strand breaks occur during PyV infection, and aspects of the DNA damage response pathway are required for efficient PyV replication (Erickson and Garcea, 2019; Heiser et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2012; Justice et al., 2019; Sowd et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The NCCR of BKPyV undergoes significant recombination events resulting from NHEJ during replication in vitro.
source: The NCCR of BKPyV undergoes significant recombination events resulting from NHEJ during replication in vitro (Zhao and Imperiale, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: JCPyV VP1 mutations identified in PML patients are associated with impaired receptor binding and infectivity.
source: JCPyV VP1 mutations identified in PML patients are associated with impaired receptor binding and infectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citations earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Only archetype JCPyV is found in the urine of PML patients, despite the presence of VP1 mutant virus in the blood and CSF of these patients.
source: Only archetype JCPyV is found in the urine of PML patients, despite the presence of VP1 mutant virus in the blood and CSF of these patients (Geoghegan et al., 2017; Gorelik et al., 2011; Maginnis et al., 2013; Reid et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The point mutations found together with the Δ297 mutation all involved a positive net change in charge.
source: The point mutations found together with the Δ297 mutation all involved a positive net change in charge (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the sequencing data.

claim: Most of the mutated residues found with Δ297 have side chains that face toward the location of receptor binding.
source: These mutations are all located near the receptor binding pocket, and most of the mutated side chains face toward the location of receptor binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Mutation of E91 to glycine causes impaired infection by promoting binding to decoy pseudoreceptors.
source: Mutation of E91 to glycine causes impaired infection by promoting binding to decoy pseudoreceptors (Bauer et al., 1999; Buch et al., 2015; Qian and Tsai, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The D295 and H297 residues face into the pore at the center of each VP1 pentamer.
source: As both the D295 and H297 residues face into the pore at the center of each VP1 pentamer, these mutations may facilitate more efficient interactions with the VP2/3 minor capsid proteins, whose C-termini extend into the pore (Chen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and a citation.

claim: The C-termini of VP2/3 minor capsid proteins extend into the pore at the center of each VP1 pentamer.
source: As both the D295 and H297 residues face into the pore at the center of each VP1 pentamer, these mutations may facilitate more efficient interactions with the VP2/3 minor capsid proteins, whose C-termini extend into the pore (Chen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The HI loop is the most common site of JCPyV VP1 mutations in PML patients.
source: The mutant viruses we identified all carried at least one mutation in the HI loop, which is also the most common site of JCPyV VP1 mutations in PML patients (Gorelik et al., 2011; Reid et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PML patients typically carry a mutant JCPyV with a single VP1 mutation.
source: PML patients typically carry a mutant JCPyV with a single VP1 mutation, rather than the double mutants we saw emerge in several mice (Supplementary file 1; Gorelik et al., 2011; Reid et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The HI loop of JCPyV (M261 to S268: 8 residues) is one residue shorter than the HI loop of MuPyV (W288 to V296: 9 residues).
source: Already the smallest external loop in VP1, the HI loop of JCPyV (M261 to S268: 8 residues) is one residue shorter than the HI loop of MuPyV (W288 to V296: 9 residues) (Liddington et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and a citation.

claim: Brain microvascular endothelial cells are susceptible to JCPyV infection.
source: Brain microvascular endothelial cells are susceptible to JCPyV infection, and could provide viral access into the CNS parenchyma (Chapagain et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: JCPyV infects choroid plexus epithelial cells.
source: JCPyV infects choroid plexus epithelial cells (Corbridge et al., 2019; Haley et al., 2015; O'Hara et al., 2018; O'Hara et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ependymal cells are permissive for productive MuPyV infection.
source: In line with this possibility is the permissivity of ependymal cells for productive MuPyV infection (Lauver et al., 2020; Mockus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A '2-hit' requirement exists for development of VP1 mutant PyVs: (1) a narrow VP1 antibody response; and (2) T cell insufficiency.
source: Our findings demonstrate a '2-hit' requirement for development of VP1 mutant PyVs: (1) a narrow VP1 antibody response; and (2) T cell insufficiency, which acts both to limit virus replication in the kidney and eliminate VP1 variants that evade antiviral antibodies.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: T cell loss leads to elevated virus replication that in the context of a narrow VP1 antibody response results in viremia by Ab-escape mutant viruses.
source: T cell loss leads to elevated virus replication that in the context of a narrow VP1 antibody response results in viremia by Ab-escape mutant viruses.

claim: Among Ab-escape variants will be those carrying the potential for neurovirulence.
